Clearly, employment for both Crows and non-Crows in Big Horn County will be higher with Westmoreland's mining activity than without it. If the Shell lease area is developed at a level of 32 million tons per year along with a third mine producing 10 million tons per year, the employment situation would be different still. Some of the most dramatic employment developments would occur if the energy conversion scenario were realized.
With a high increase in the Crow Labor Force Participation Rate and no out-migration of Crow workers, the demand for Crow workers must keep abreast of the increasing labor force or a high rate of unemployment will result.
Under the assumption that Crow labor force participation rates will slowly rise as opportunities improve, and assuming that 75 percent of the mining related jobs are available to Crows, the growth of the Crow labor force quickly outstrips the employment opportunities offered by Westmoreland's most probable level of development (Scenario 1) alone. Under the converging rate and with no other Crow coal development, this level of Westmoreland activity maintains reasonably full utilization of Crow labor until 1980. The Crow unemployment rate starts rising rapidly in 1980, however, from a level of 10 percent to 40 percent in 1990, to 50 percent in 2000.
